summary:
This evaluation covered 12 "ecr-guard" eval scenarios testing an ECR lifecycle-policy guard agent. Two of the 12 evals were negative-trigger tests (should_trigger: false) and were marked skipped for all dimensions — both variants correctly had the behavior fire (trigger_fired 1/1) with no further scoring needed, so they don't contribute evidence either way. One eval ("ecr-guard-draft-policy-preview") only produced scorable assertion data for with_skill (without_skill's assertions are null/inconclusive), and another ("ecr-guard-production-tag-catch-all") likewise only scored with_skill, and a third ("ecr-guard-unexpected-deletion-postmortem") only scored without_skill. These asymmetric-data evals limit direct comparison for those specific tasks.

Across the remaining evals with both variants scored, overall "expected output" match was low for both variants in almost every eval — frequently 0/1 for both, with a mix of high and medium confidence ratings (so the judgments themselves are reasonably trustworthy even though the outcomes were poor). Assertion-level pass rates were generally low to moderate for both variants (often in the 15–50% range), and the pattern across eval files is consistent: most individual assertions are either "always_fails" (neither variant satisfies a specific requirement, e.g. required report sections, rating vocabulary, Check Matrix formatting, SIMULATED/AUTHORITATIVE labeling, exact expiring-image counts) or "always_passes" (both variants handle some requirements fine, e.g. not reporting write APIs as called, listing certain tag families correctly). These shared-fail and shared-pass assertions indicate the measured differences are concentrated in a smaller set of assertions, rather than a broad quality gap between the variants.

Where the two variants did diverge on individual assertions, the direction was mixed rather than one-sided: in "ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list," without_skill passed "full report, not a summary" while with_skill failed it, but with_skill passed "does not call anything safe outside a verdict row" while without_skill failed it. In "ecr-guard-gap-h2-safe-to-leave" and "ecr-guard-account-sweep," with_skill passed a couple of assertions (AccessDenied handling, rating vocabulary) that without_skill failed, while without_skill passed an assertion about not ending with an unwanted offer, or about collecting the in-use inventory, that with_skill failed. In the "evaluation" sub-evals (five-rule-expiry-list, v230-in-use, push-correlated-event-excluded, cloudtrail-consumer-pull-in-use), results were close and mixed: with_skill edged ahead on some individual checks (e.g., listing rc survivors, presenting a protective rule JSON) while without_skill edged ahead on others (e.g., explaining push-correlation timing, correctly setting Repository Rating to AtRisk in two of the scenarios). Overall assertion pass-rate percentages in these four evals were close (with_skill 40-50% vs without_skill 38-60%), without a consistent direction.

Runtime and cost varied considerably by eval and did not track a consistent pattern: in some evals with_skill was much slower and costlier (e.g., "gap-h1" 56s/$0.47 vs without_skill's 3m25s/$1.71 — here without_skill was slower/costlier; "gap-h2" with_skill 7m28s/$3.73 vs without_skill 2m56s/$1.47 — with_skill slower/costlier; "account-sweep" with_skill 8m13s/$4.09 vs without_skill 1m43s/$0.86 — with_skill much slower/costlier; "production-tag-catch-all" with_skill 36s/$0.31 vs without_skill 7s/$0.06 — with_skill slower). So the faster/cheaper variant alternates across evals, meaning no consistent cost or speed advantage was observed for either variant across the full set.

Quality-comparison pairs (direct quality judging) were skipped for every eval (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped each), and output-consistency data was null throughout, so no information is available on output quality head-to-head comparisons or run-to-run consistency for either variant — these are both absent dimensions rather than indicating a problem for one side.

In sum, both variants struggled similarly on the core expected-output and most assertions across this ECR-guard task suite (many assertions always failed for both, pointing to shared gaps, likely in the agent behavior or possibly in assertion strictness rather than a one-sided variant weakness), with no consistent lead for either variant on the specific assertions, cost, or runtime, and no quality-comparison or consistency data available to supplement the picture.

ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on a single chat task involving an ECR lifecycle policy report. Overall results show both variants struggling similarly, with no clear separation in outcome.

Key findings:
- The trigger-fired check (whether the tested behavior occurred at all) failed (0/1), which applies to the eval as a whole and is a flag that the underlying scenario/behavior may not have engaged as intended for either variant.
- Expected-output match was 0/1 (failed) for both without_skill and with_skill, and this was measured with high confidence for both, so this is a fairly solid (not low-confidence) finding that neither variant produced the expected output on this task.
- Assertion-level pass rates were identical in aggregate: 2/11 (18%) for both variants. Breaking this down:
  - 7 of 11 assertions failed for both variants ("always_fails") — covering things like stating AUTHORITATIVE/SIMULATED status, attempting or explaining the lifecycle preview call, giving per-image verdicts with evidence, correctly handling in-use/pull-window images, handling AccessDenied cases, required section headings, valid Repository Rating values, and the full 15-row check matrix. These indicate shared gaps in the underlying behavior or the assertions' strictness, not a difference between variants.
  - 1 assertion ("no write API reported as called") passed for both variants — a dimension that doesn't differentiate them.
  - 2 assertions diverged: without_skill passed "the response is the full report, not a prose summary/offer" (with_skill failed this one), while with_skill passed "the response does not state any expiring image is safe/not a concern" (without_skill failed this one). These are the only points of divergence, each favoring a different variant, and confidence on these was medium-to-high.
- No quality-comparison pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh here.
- Output consistency across repeated runs was not available (null) for either variant, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed.
- On cost and runtime, with_skill was notably faster (~56s vs ~3m25s) and cheaper (~$0.47 vs ~$1.71) than without_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (3.7% vs 4.1%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall picture: This is a case where the aggregate assertion pass rate is identical between variants, but that aggregate hides two individual assertions where the variants diverge in opposite directions (one point each). The majority of assertions failed for both variants, suggesting the core task behavior (lifecycle preview status reporting, per-image verdicts, required report structure) was not met by either variant, and the expected-output and trigger-fired failures reinforce that neither produced the full expected result. Variant_b completed faster and at lower cost, while without_skill took substantially longer and cost more, but with no quality-comparison data available, it's not possible to say whether that extra time/cost for without_skill corresponded to any measurable quality benefit beyond the single assertion it won. Given the lack of quality-pair data and consistency data, and the shared high failure rate across most assertions, this result set should be read as showing largely similar (and largely unmet) performance for both variants, with a couple of small, offsetting differences and a cost/runtime tradeoff favoring with_skill.

ecr-guard-gap-h2-safe-to-leave.summary:
Both variants were tested on a single chat task, so all findings here come from one trial each and should be read as a snapshot rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The trigger behavior fired (1/1). On the "expected output" check, with_skill passed (1/1, medium confidence) while without_skill failed (0/1, high confidence). Since without_skill's failing judgment was made with high confidence, this is a reasonably solid signal that without_skill did not meet the expected output in this run, while with_skill did — though with only one data point, it's not yet a trend.

Assertions: Overall pass rates were identical for both variants (2/9, 22%). Looking at the per-assertion breakdown:
- Three assertions always failed for both variants (full structured report format, lastRecordedPullTime handling, and explanation of direct-pull visibility/CloudTrail lag) — these point to behaviors neither variant exhibited, suggesting either a shared agent limitation or an assertion/task calibration issue rather than a difference between variants.
- Two regex-based assertions (Repository Rating fixed values, fixed verdict vocabulary) also failed for both variants, reinforcing that the report's formatting/vocabulary requirements weren't met by either.
- One assertion (no write API reported) passed for both — this is confirmed shared behavior, not a differentiator.
- One assertion split in with_skill's favor: correctly handling AccessDenied on batch:DescribeJobDefinitions by marking affected images as Expiring-Unknown and listing under Not Assessed — with_skill passed, without_skill failed (both at high confidence).
- One assertion split in without_skill's favor: not ending with an offer to modify/delete/investigate further — without_skill passed (medium confidence), with_skill failed (high confidence).

So on the only two assertions where the variants actually differed, each won one, pointing to a genuine tradeoff rather than one variant being uniformly stronger on assertions.

Metrics: with_skill took notably longer (7m28s vs 2m56s, about 4.5 minutes more) and cost more (~$3.73 vs ~$1.47, roughly 2.5x). Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.6% vs 4.2%), with no compaction for either. This is a clear cost/speed tradeoff, with without_skill being faster and cheaper.

Quality comparison and consistency: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct head-to-head quality judgment available. Output consistency data is also absent (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, the picture is mixed and based on very limited data (a single task instance): with_skill met the overall expected output in this run while without_skill did not (high confidence on the failure), and with_skill also handled the AccessDenied/Not-Assessed case correctly while without_skill did not; conversely, without_skill correctly avoided ending with an unwanted offer while with_skill did not, and without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Several core formatting/content assertions (report structure, verdict vocabulary, rating values, lastRecordedPullTime and direct-pull explanations) failed for both variants, indicating shared gaps that are independent of the variant difference. No quality-comparison or consistency data was available to weigh further.

ecr-guard-account-sweep.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested an ECR/ECS repository-inventory reporting behavior. The triggering condition for the test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: Neither variant met the overall expected output (0/1 for both). Variant_b's failure was assessed with high confidence, while without_skill's was assessed with only medium confidence, so without_skill's failing grade is somewhat less certain than with_skill's.

Assertions (8 total, both variants passing 2/8 = 25%): Looking behind the aggregate tie, the pattern differs by assertion:
- Four assertions failed for both variants (Account Summary table content/no region prompt, correct AtRisk/Indeterminate/Attention/Healthy ordering, handling of repos with no lifecycle policy, and full per-repo detail sections for non-Healthy repos). These are "always_fails" patterns, suggesting the underlying behavior or the assertion itself needs work for both variants.
- One regex assertion ("Account Summary heading is present") failed for both.
- One regex assertion ("No write API reported as called") passed for both — a check that doesn't differentiate the variants.
- One LLM-judged assertion (stating in-use inventory collected once per Region and listing source status) passed for without_skill but failed for with_skill (both medium confidence).
- One regex assertion ("rating vocabulary used") passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill.
So each variant uniquely passed one assertion the other failed, netting the same overall pass rate despite differing on substance.

Metrics: without_skill was notably faster (1m43s vs 8m13s) and cheaper ($0.86 vs $4.09) than with_skill, with slightly lower context-window utilization (4.2% vs 6.0%); neither used compaction.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality judgment available to weigh against the cost/runtime difference.

Output consistency: Not measured for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability is unknown.

Overall, this is a case where both variants failed the primary expected-output check and tied on aggregate assertion pass rate, but the two variants failed/passed different individual assertions, meaning the tie conceals some real behavioral differences. Variant_a completed much faster and at lower cost, but with no quality-comparison data and no consistency data, this cost/speed difference cannot be weighed against output quality. The confidence levels attached to the expected-output judgments (medium for without_skill, high for with_skill) suggest the without_skill result is a bit less certain than with_skill's.

ecr-guard-draft-policy-preview.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about reviewing an ECR/ECS lifecycle policy, and the data available is quite limited.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior-under-test trigger did not fire (0/1), and expected_output was not met for with_skill (0/1, with high confidence in that judgment, so this is a fairly reliable negative finding). Variant_b's expected_output also shows 0/1, though no avg_confidence is reported for it, so that result is less well-supported than with_skill's. Neither variant met the expected output in this single trial.

Assertions: Only with_skill has assertion-level data (without_skill's assertion results are null/not measured, so no direct comparison is possible on this dimension). Variant_a passed just 1 of 7 assertions (14%). The one it passed, with high confidence, was a "does not apply the draft policy / does not call PutLifecyclePolicy" safety check — a reasonable guardrail outcome. It failed the other six, including checks about evaluating the correct (draft) policy and labeling the source, stating AUTHORITATIVE vs SIMULATED preview status, correctly identifying the expiring image set, raising the production-tag finding (P4), including a source label via regex, and producing a 15-row check matrix. Most of these failures were judged with medium-to-high confidence, suggesting the shortfalls are real rather than artifacts of weak measurement. Because without_skill has no assertion data at all, we cannot say whether it would have done better, worse, or the same on these specific checks — this is missing data, not a sign without_skill underperformed.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no head-to-head quality signal between the two variants for this task.

Runtime and cost: The two variants were very close — with_skill ran ~41s at ~$0.34, without_skill ~42s at ~$0.35, and context-window utilization was similarly low for both (3.7% vs 4.0%, no compaction for either). These differences are negligible and do not meaningfully distinguish the variants.

Output consistency: Not measured for either variant (both null), so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, the only dimension with substantive data is with_skill's assertion/expected-output performance, which was weak (passing only a safety-related assertion while failing the substantive content checks), and with_skill's expected-output miss was high-confidence. Variant_b essentially lacks comparable data across assertions, quality, and consistency, so this result should be read as a one-sided look at with_skill's shortcomings in this task rather than a balanced comparison between the two variants. Runtime and cost were effectively equivalent.

ecr-guard-production-tag-catch-all.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about ECR lifecycle policy rules for protecting prod-*/release-* images. The data available is quite limited, and several important dimensions could not be measured for without_skill at all.

Key observations:

- Trigger / expected output: The overall trigger behavior under test did not fire (0/1), and expected_output failed for both with_skill (0/1, high confidence) and without_skill (0/1). So on the core "did it meet the expected output" measure, both variants failed, and the result is reasonably high-confidence for with_skill, meaning this isn't a weak signal — it's a genuine shared shortfall.

- Assertions: Only with_skill has per-assertion data; without_skill shows null for every assertion, so no direct comparison is possible on individual criteria. Variant_b passed 3 of 6 assertions (50%). Of note:
  - It passed the two regex-based checks (presence of a protective rule JSON with tagPatternList, and no write API call reported) and one LLM-judged assertion about explaining the tagStatus/newest-10 protection mechanism (medium confidence).
  - It failed three LLM-judged assertions (all high confidence) covering: using one rule per tag family with correct priority/AND semantics, reporting which current images are in the expiring set with verdicts, and stating that the operator (not the agent) applies the rule after a preview. These failures point to specific gaps in with_skill's response rather than an ambiguous judgment, but since without_skill has no assertion data, we cannot tell whether it would have passed or failed these same checks.

- Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no quality-based comparison available between the two variants.

- Runtime and cost: without_skill was notably faster (~7s vs ~36s) and cheaper (~$0.06 vs ~$0.31) than with_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~3.7–3.9%), with no compaction events for either.

- Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null).

Overall, the only dimension with a direct head-to-head signal is runtime/cost, where without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. However, this cannot be weighed against quality or assertion performance for without_skill, since that data is simply absent (not scored as zero, but not measured). Both variants failed the expected-output check for this task, with that failure being relatively high-confidence for with_skill. Variant_b's partial assertion pass pattern (passing format/safety-related checks but failing more substantive correctness checks about rule design, current-state reporting, and operator-approval framing) is a useful but isolated finding, since there is no without_skill data to compare it against. In short, this is a thin, partially-measured comparison: the clearest, most reliable fact is the speed/cost gap favoring without_skill, while correctness and quality remain largely unresolved for without_skill and only partially characterized for with_skill.

The one that passed (with high confidence) was that the response avoided performing or offering to perform a re-push, restore, deletion, or policy change itself — a safe-behavior check. Overall, this single eval provides substantive data only for without_skill, and that data points to the task's expected output and most content-specific assertions not being met, with confidence in the underlying checks ranging from medium to high. ecr-guard-evaluation-five-rule-expiry-li.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about simulating an ECR lifecycle policy. Overall, the data points to a scenario where neither variant met the full expected output, and both share most of the same strengths and weaknesses.

Trigger and expected output: The trigger-fired check and the expected_output check both failed (0/1) for both without_skill and with_skill, with high confidence in that judgment. This means the specific behavior being tested essentially did not fire or succeed for either variant — this looks like a shortfall in the underlying task/behavior itself (or a very strict expectation) rather than something distinguishing the two variants.

Assertions (10 total, mix of LLM-graded and regex-graded):
- Both variants fail identically on 4 assertions: stating "exactly 12 images expire," explaining the rule-priority interaction (rules 100/30/40/20), stating the image count as a count rather than a tag, and including the "SIMULATED" label. These are "always_fails" patterns, indicating these specific behaviors need work regardless of variant.
- Both variants pass identically on 4 assertions: listing build-8–12 and rc-0.1–0.4 as survivors, listing nightly-20261001 as expiring, listing build-1–7, and listing v2.1.0–v2.4.0. These are shared strengths and don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion ("The rc images are mentioned as survivors") passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill — this is the only point of divergence found in the assertion set.
- Net effect: with_skill passed 5/10 assertions vs without_skill's 4/10, a one-assertion difference driven entirely by the rc-images point.

Runtime, cost, and context usage were effectively identical between the two variants (both ~0s, ~$0.00, ~3.6% context utilization, no compaction) — no meaningful tradeoff in efficiency.

Quality comparison and consistency: The head-to-head quality comparison had 0 pairs evaluated and 1 pair skipped, so no direct quality judgment is available. Output consistency across repeated runs was not measured (null) for both variants. These are gaps in the data rather than indications of poor performance.

In summary: both variants largely behaved the same, failing the same four assertions (including the core SIMULATED-label and rule-priority explanation points) and the overarching expected-output check, while passing the same four more basic listing assertions. The only observed difference is that with_skill also correctly mentioned rc images as survivors while without_skill did not, giving with_skill a slightly higher assertion pass rate (5/10 vs 4/10). No runtime, cost, or consistency differences were observed, and quality and consistency comparisons could not be computed due to skipped/missing data, so this should be treated as a narrow, low-leverage difference rather than a broad performance gap.
